items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “secularisation”, and give one example.
items.answer: The process by which religious thinking, practices and institutions lose social significance (Wilson). Example: falling church attendance and religious influence on law.

items.stem: Explain the difference between “disengagement” and “secularisation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Disengagement: the withdrawal of religious institutions from wider society and the state (e.g. churches losing control over education and welfare). Secularisation: the process by which religious thinking, practices and institutions lose social significance (Wilson) (e.g. falling church attendance and religious influence on law).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A government near Lisbon legalises divorce and same-sex marriage despite opposition from religious leaders, and removes religious education from the national curriculum. Suggest how a religious market sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Religious market theory: religion is a market: when there is competition and choice, religious organisations meet people’s needs and religiosity stays strong (Stark and Bainbridge).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In Muscat, religious weddings have fallen from 70% to 20% of all weddings in forty years, and most schools that were once run by churches are now run by the state. Explain how a religious market sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Religious market theory: religion is a market: when there is competition and choice, religious organisations meet people’s needs and religiosity stays strong (Stark and Bainbridge).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A government near Mumbai legalises divorce and same-sex marriage despite opposition from religious leaders, and removes religious education from the national curriculum. Compare how postmodernist and functionalist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: religion is not disappearing but changing: it becomes individual, private and consumer-based (Davie, Lyon). Functionalism: structural differentiation means specialised institutions take over religion’s functions, so its role becomes more limited (Parsons).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating changes in religious attendance over fifty years. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in religious attendance over fifty years but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research changes in religious attendance over fifty years.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in religious attendance over fifty years but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: What is the difference between “structural differentiation” and “disenchantment”?

items.stem: Chloe is planning a study of private religious belief among people who do not attend services. Evaluate the use of case studies for this research.

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying religiosity in countries at different levels of development.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying religiosity in countries at different levels of development but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful covert participant observation is for studying how religious leaders feel about their declining influence.
items.answer: Strengths: it can give access to closed or deviant groups who would refuse an overt researcher; because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided. Limitations: secretly recording sensitive behaviour without consent raises serious ethical problems of deception and harm; it involves deception and lack of informed consent, which breaks ethical guidelines. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how religious leaders feel about their declining influence but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: In Colombo, religious weddings have fallen from 70% to 20% of all weddings in forty years, and most schools that were once run by churches are now run by the state. Suggest how a religious market sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Religious market theory: religion is a market: when there is competition and choice, religious organisations meet people’s needs and religiosity stays strong (Stark and Bainbridge).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Official statistics on religious practice in a country near Karachi are shown below. Table: religious practice in a country | 1980 | 2020. Religious weddings (% of weddings) | 68% | 41%. Children baptised or given a religious naming ceremony (%) | 53% | 32%. Adults attending weekly (%) | 20% | 14%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Religious weddings (% of weddings) change between 1980 and 2020?
items.answer: -27 percentage points
items.markingKey: 41 − 68 = -27 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: The table shows official data on religious practice in one country. Table: religious practice in a country | 1980 | 2020. Religious weddings (% of weddings) | 60% | 31%. Children baptised or given a religious naming ceremony (%) | 62% | 34%. Adults attending weekly (%) | 13% | 6%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Religious weddings (% of weddings) between 1980 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Calculate the gap between Religious weddings (% of weddings) and Children baptised or given a religious naming ceremony (%) in 1980 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened.
items.answer: (a) (31 − 60) ÷ 60 × 100 = -48.3%. (b) 1980: 2 percentage points; 2020: 3 percentage points; the gap widened.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (31 − 60) ÷ 60 × 100; 1 mark for -48.3% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark each gap (2 and 3); 1 mark for “widened”. [3]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) to research changes in religious attendance over fifty years.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow sociologists to study families and communities in the past that cannot be observed now; they give an insight into people’s feelings and meanings in their own words, so validity can be high. Limitations: they cannot show how common a pattern is across a society; their meaning must be interpreted by the researcher, which may introduce bias. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in religious attendance over fifty years but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Official statistics on religious practice in a country near Bangkok are shown below. Table: religious practice in a country | 1980 | 2020. Religious weddings (% of weddings) | 62% | 27%. Children baptised or given a religious naming ceremony (%) | 54% | 31%. Adults attending weekly (%) | 18% | 10%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Religious weddings (% of weddings) between 1980 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that secularisation is taking place.
items.answer: (a) (27 − 62) ÷ 62 × 100 = -56.5%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for Religious weddings (% of weddings), Children baptised or given a religious naming ceremony (%), Adults attending weekly (%); Children baptised or given a religious naming ceremony (%) had the highest figure for 2020. Rationalisation and individualism weaken religious practice. Qualifications: Practice is not the same as belief; believing without belonging; vicarious religion; religion grows in other forms and other parts of the world. The data also come from official statistics of 3 couples in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (27 − 62) ÷ 62 × 100; 1 mark for -56.5% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that religion is like a market in which competition and choice increase participation?
items.answer: Religious market theory
items.markingKey: Religious market theory: the view that religion is like a market in which competition and choice increase participation. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “believing without belonging”.
items.answer: Davie’s idea that many people hold religious beliefs but do not attend or belong to religious organisations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: Davie’s idea that many people hold religious beliefs but do not attend or belong to religious organisations. [1]

items.stem: Explain the religious market theory explanation of religiosity.
items.answer: Religion is a market; when there is competition and choice, organisations improve their “products” and meet needs, so participation rises (USA); state monopolies reduce participation (Europe).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each point up to 4. [4]

items.stem: Lina surveyed 800 adults of different ages in Madrid. Table: adults (%) | Aged 65 and over | Aged 18-34. Believe in God | 67% | 33%. Pray at least monthly | 60% | 35%. Attend services at least monthly | 25% | 7%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Aged 65 and over and Aged 18-34 for Pray at least monthly (Aged 18-34 minus Aged 65 and over)?
items.answer: -25 percentage points
items.markingKey: 35 − 60 = -25 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Nadia, a sociology student, is designing a project on private religious belief among people who do not attend services. Explain two limitations of using covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: 1. It involves deception and lack of informed consent, which breaks ethical guidelines. 2. The study cannot be repeated, so reliability is low.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to private religious belief among people who do not attend services. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful participant observation is for studying private religious belief among people who do not attend services.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; the researcher sees what people actually do in their natural setting, not just what they say, so validity is high. Limitations: it is very difficult to observe private behaviour inside homes; the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying private religious belief among people who do not attend services but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a feeling that survival is secure enough to be taken for granted?
items.answer: Existential security
items.markingKey: Existential security: a feeling that survival is secure enough to be taken for granted. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “The world as a whole is becoming less religious because populations in religious countries are shrinking.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Populations in poorer, more religious countries are growing faster, so the world as a whole is becoming more religious.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain Norris and Inglehart’s argument that religion declines in secure, wealthy societies but remains strong in poor, insecure ones, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Their existential security theory explains why the world as a whole is becoming more religious: poorer populations are growing faster. Criticism: The USA is rich but religious.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Weberian theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The table shows international survey results on religiosity. Table: adults (%) | Say religion is “very important” | Attend services weekly. Low-income countries | 81% | 60%. Middle-income countries | 55% | 27%. High-income countries | 19% | 11%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Say religion is “very important” and Attend services weekly for Middle-income countries (Attend services weekly minus Say religion is “very important”)?
items.answer: -28 percentage points
items.markingKey: 27 − 55 = -28 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: In a fast-growing city near Doha, new Pentecostal churches open every month, attracting migrants from rural areas with lively worship and help finding jobs. Explain how a Weberian sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religion declines where people are secure; global religiosity reflects insecurity and population growth (Norris and Inglehart).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: The table shows international survey results on religiosity. Table: adults (%) | Say religion is “very important” | Attend services weekly. Low-income countries | 81% | 47%. Middle-income countries | 57% | 29%. High-income countries | 15% | 9%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Say religion is “very important” and Attend services weekly for Low-income countries. (b) Explain one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that secularisation is linked to economic development.
items.answer: (a) 47 − 81 = -34 percentage points (Attend services weekly compared with Say religion is “very important”). (b) Response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Attend services weekly than for Say religion is “very important” among Low-income countries, Middle-income countries, High-income countries; Low-income countries had the highest figure for Attend services weekly. Existential insecurity in poorer countries (Norris and Inglehart). Qualifications: Exceptions such as the USA and Gulf states; survey questions may mean different things in different cultures; averages hide variation. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 3 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 81 and 47; 1 mark for 34 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]
